questions.prompt: Which traversal finds the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph?

options.text: Neither — you need Dijkstra even for unweighted graphs

questions.explanation: BFS visits vertices in order of distance from the source, so the first time it reaches a vertex is along a fewest-edges path.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of BFS or DFS using an adjacency list?
questions.explanation: Each vertex is dequeued/visited once and each edge is examined a constant number of times, giving O(V + E).

questions.prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space
An adjacency matrix uses O(V + E) space

questions.explanation: BFS is queue-based, DFS is stack/recursion-based, and adjacency lists are O(V+E). An adjacency matrix is O(V²), so (d) is false.

questions.prompt: To avoid revisiting nodes and looping forever on cycles, a graph traversal marks each node as ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: A visited set records explored vertices so the traversal terminates even when the graph has cycles.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of one BFS iteration (starting from an initialized queue).

items.text: Dequeue the next node from the front
For each unvisited neighbor, mark it visited and enqueue it
Repeat until the queue is empty

questions.explanation: BFS repeatedly dequeues a node, processes it, and enqueues its unvisited neighbors (marking them visited on enqueue) until the queue drains.

questions.prompt: Match each item with its property.

pairs.right: O(V + E) space; good for sparse graphs

questions.explanation: BFS and DFS differ by frontier structure and use; the two representations trade space for edge-lookup speed.
